To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
priority setting is a key process in the evaluation of health technologies, and that existing prioritization models are inadequate to support decision making.

(1) priority setting is a key step in the process of evaluating a health intervention; (2) a number of explicit models have been developed in recent years to support the priority setting process; and (3) the models have not been widely adopted in practice, because of a number of important limitations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new model that is able to address the limitations of existing conceptual frameworks.
the development of a new model for setting priorities for health technology assessment (HTA).
the gap that exists between the theory of priority setting and its practice, and how this gap can be bridged.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the existing conceptual models of priority setting have been of little use in practice.
the existing conceptual models of priority setting are not suitable for guiding the evaluation of health technology in a research portfolio context.
there is a lack of consensus about the criteria that should be used to prioritize evaluations of health interventions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have not yet developed a formal theory of priority setting for evaluation.
the models developed to date do not adequately capture the complexities of priority setting.
we have developed a framework for the prioritisation of research and development (R&D) projects that is suitable for the purpose of supporting cost containment and distributional objectives.
The main takeaway from our work is that
priority setting for health technology assessment is a complex task that requires more than the use of a single model.
the evaluation of health care interventions is an inherently political process, in which the role of theory is limited.

the development and application of formal models of priority setting in health technology assessment should be guided by the following principles: the model should be developed for the specific purpose of prioritizing evaluations; it should address priority setting in the context of a research portfolio; and it should be based on the assumption that priority setting is an incremental, iterative process.
